messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi, a 37-year-old South Asian male and licensed psychologist, has been struggling with the aftermath of a terrorist attack that occurred eight months ago. On that fateful day, Ravi was attending a conference at his university when an explosion rocked the building. The chaos was immediate; people were screaming, bodies were falling, and the sound of gunfire echoed through the halls. As he tried to navigate through the smoke-filled corridors, Ravi felt a complete loss of control over his surroundings. His heart pounded in his chest, and every cell in his body screamed for safety. The experience left deep scars that have only grown more pronounced over time. Night after night, Ravi is haunted by the memory of that day. The darkness brings back the feeling of being trapped and overwhelmed, unable to protect himself or others. He wakes up in a cold sweat, terrified and disoriented, believing that he can't stop bad things from happening to him. In an attempt to cope with these overwhelming feelings, Ravi has adopted several maladaptive strategies. He tries to avoid anything that could be stressful, often skipping social events and professional conferences for fear of being caught off guard again. The weight of this isolation is palpable; his once vibrant social life has dwindled to almost nothing. His colleagues have noticed the change in him but haven’t been able to penetrate his guarded demeanor. During the day, Ravi finds solace in drifting into a world of his own making—a fantasy escape where he can control everything and nothing bad happens. These mental retreats are brief respites from the anxiety that follows him everywhere. They provide temporary relief but do little to address the underlying issues. In the evenings, when the memories become too much to bear, Ravi turns to alcohol. The numbing effects of intoxication offer a fleeting sense of calm and control over his thoughts. Over time, he has increased his consumption, leading to more frequent episodes of drinking to cope with his anxiety. This pattern has begun to affect his work life; he often arrives late or leaves early, citing fatigue as the reason. The trauma has also left Ravi feeling unrecognizable to himself. The person he once was—a confident and driven professional—has been replaced by someone who is plagued by fear and self-doubt. His wife, Priya, has noticed these changes but struggles with how to help him. They used to spend their evenings discussing work or planning weekend activities together, but now those conversations are filled with his anxieties about the world being a dangerous place. Despite his efforts to avoid stressors and escape through fantasy and substance use, Ravi's symptoms have only worsened over time. The combination of sleepless nights and frequent bouts of drinking has taken a toll on both his physical health and professional life. His colleagues have expressed concern, but he remains hesitant to reveal the true extent of his struggles. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was an incident at work where a colleague’s phone rang suddenly, mimicking the sound of gunfire from that day. The sheer panic and fear that overtook him were too much to bear in front of others. In that moment, he realized that the only way to reclaim his life was to confront these fears head-on. Ravi is most afraid of becoming a shell of himself, unable to function or enjoy anything anymore. He hopes that with help, he can regain control and find a sense of safety again. The journey will be challenging, but Ravi is determined to rebuild the person he once was and reclaim his life from the shadow of that traumatic event.
